question.prompt: There exists a unique strictly increasing sequence of nonnegative integers \(a_1 \lt a_2 \lt \cdots \lt a_k\) such that \[\frac{2^{289} + 1}{2^{17} + 1} = 2^{a_1} + 2^{a_2} + \cdots + 2^{a_k}.\] What is \(k?\)

solutions.title: Expand into blocks of powers
solutions.explanation:
The number \(k\) counts the \(1\)-digits in the quotient's binary expansion. Since \(289=17\cdot17\), we can expose those digits by setting \(X=2^{17}\).

Then
\[
\frac{2^{289}+1}{2^{17}+1}
=\frac{X^{17}+1}{X+1}
=X^{16}-X^{15}+X^{14}-X^{13}+\cdots+X^2-X+1.
\]
To verify the last equality, multiply the alternating sum by \(X+1\). Every intermediate power cancels, leaving \(X^{17}+1\).

Group the terms into eight differences and the final \(1\):
\[
(X^{16}-X^{15})+(X^{14}-X^{13})+\cdots+(X^2-X)+1.
\]
Each difference has the form \(X^{m+1}-X^m\), where \(m\) is one of \(1,3,5,\ldots,15\). The geometric sum identity gives
\[
2^{17}-1=1+2+2^2+\cdots+2^{16}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
X^{m+1}-X^m
&=2^{17m}(2^{17}-1)\\
&=2^{17m}+2^{17m+1}+\cdots+2^{17m+16}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each difference therefore contributes \(17\) distinct powers of \(2\).

The exponent ranges are
\[
17\text{ through }33,\quad51\text{ through }67,\quad\ldots,\quad255\text{ through }271.
\]
These eight ranges are disjoint, so no powers repeat and no binary carries occur. The final \(1=2^0\) is outside all the ranges and contributes one more term.

Thus \(k=8\cdot17+1=\boxed{137}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutions.title: Track binary carries
solutions.explanation:
Multiplication by \(2^{17}+1\) adds a number to a copy shifted \(17\) binary places. Tracking the carries determines the quotient's digits.

Call the quotient \(N\). Then
\[
N+2^{17}N=2^{289}+1.
\]
Number binary positions starting at \(0\), so position \(i\) has value \(2^i\). We seek the number of \(1\)-digits of \(N\). Also,
\[
2^{289}+1<2^{272}(2^{17}+1),
\]
so \(N<2^{272}\). Its digits at positions \(272\) and higher are therefore zero.

The required sum has a \(1\) only at positions \(0\) and \(289\). At position \(0\), the digit of \(N\) must be \(1\). At positions \(1\) through \(16\), its digits must be zero because neither the shifted copy nor a carry contributes.

At position \(17\), the shifted copy contributes the original position-\(0\) digit, which is \(1\). To obtain a zero in the sum, \(N\) must also have a \(1\) here. Binary \(1+1\) writes a zero and carries \(1\) to the next position.

At positions \(18\) through \(33\), the shifted digits are zero. Each incoming carry is \(1\), so each digit of \(N\) must be \(1\), producing another zero and another carry.

From position \(34\) onward, there is still an incoming carry of \(1\). To make the sum digit zero, the digit of \(N\) must be opposite to its digit \(17\) places earlier. Indeed, the current digit, the shifted digit, and the carry then total \(2\). This forces alternating blocks of \(17\) zeros and \(17\) ones.

The blocks of ones are at positions
\[
17+34j\text{ through }33+34j,
\qquad j=0,1,\ldots,7.
\]
The last block ends at \(271\). At positions \(272\) through \(288\), the digits of \(N\) are zero, while the shifted digits are those last \(17\) ones. Together with the carry, each column again totals \(2\). At position \(289\), both number digits are zero, so the incoming carry gives the required final \(1\) and stops.

Thus \(N\) has eight blocks of \(17\) ones, together with the one at position \(0\). Therefore
\[
k=8\cdot17+1=\boxed{137},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
